lesson_title: The Kettle the Size of a Suburb
hook_text: Your phone is charging on a kettle. A kettle the size of a suburb, burning coal in Mpumalanga right now.
clip_script: Strip away the chimneys and the pylons, and a coal power station is your kitchen kettle scaled up until it runs a nation. At home, the element heats water and steam rattles the lid. In Mpumalanga, coal ground fine as flour burns at 1 400 degrees, boiling water inside kilometres of tubes that line the furnace walls. But this steam does not rattle a lid — it blasts a turbine into a 3 000-revolutions-per-minute spin, and that shaft turns a giant magnet inside coils of wire. That is all a generator is: motion becoming electricity. Then transformers pump the voltage up to 400 000 volts, because electricity travels long distances with fewer losses at high pressure — and Gauteng is far away. Now three secrets. Those huge funnel-shaped towers? The white clouds above them are not smoke — they are water vapour from cooling the used steam; the real smoke leaves by the tall thin stacks. The stations huddle ON the coalfields because wire is cheaper than rail: send the electricity travelling, not the coal. And the sobering one: of every three coal trucks burned, only about one truck's worth becomes electricity. The other two warm the sky. Eighty per cent of South Africa runs on this kettle — which is exactly why the fight over its future is the biggest energy story in the country.
visual_style: A kitchen kettle morphing scale-step by scale-step into Kendal power station; cutaway animation of pulverised coal, glowing boiler tubes, spinning turbine and magnet; a map of pylons streaming light from Mpumalanga to Gauteng; three coal trucks with two fading into heat shimmer.
mood: Wonder at the machinery, sobered by the final count.
pacing: Playful morph at the open, driving mechanical rhythm through the energy chain, a slow held beat on the two lost trucks.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and follow every volt from coalface to phone charger.
